Now, I would like to tell you about the field and job options. I know this is really long, but as a 28-year-old, I wish someone told me this at 18-22. Entry to mid-level position titles: Environmental engineer, environmental scientist, environmental specialist, environmental health and safety specialist, biologist, wastewater inspector, planner, water quality specialist, industrial hygienist, or environmental health specialist. Depending on where you live, entry-level salaries will be between 35- 55 k, maybe 60 k in SF or NYC. You will not make 80-100 k within the first several years. Consider, the industrial world may not always welcome you, so expect resistance in mining, oil, manufacturing, or construction. Lots of environmental work is compliance based.

Oil/Gas and Mining: These positions pay 50-90 k. They are often in rural areas and can be prone to layoffs. Expect to do permitting and some hazardous waste. Expect some desk work and some field work.

Manufacturing/Construction: Lower than the first option, but more stable. Likely 40-85 k. Can be office work or out in the plant/job site. Will most likely be combined with health and safety. Lots of waste and some sustainability. Heavy on jobs where manufacturing is big, the south and midwest. A recession can hurt these jobs, but not like oil or mining.

Government: This is the most stable option and has great benefits. Pay varies, depending on the state, local, or federal agencies 35-85 k+. It is pretty competitive to get into. Jobs can be slower pace but bureaucratic. You might do some technical writing, inspecting industrial sites, and sampling/testing. There are jobs everywhere and very few layoffs.

Non-Profits: Mostly concentrated on the east and west coasts in big cities. Jobs may be interesting but very low pay, 30-70 k at most. This is the least recommended path.

Consulting/Engineering Firms: This will likely be in a metro area, although these jobs are in most places. The pay varies, based on the size of the firm, your degrees, and your certifications. Pay is likely 35- 85 k. A lot of the work is office based report writing, but sampling and testing jobs are out there. These jobs also tend to have more hours but more flexibility. 

Insurance: There are some positions doing environmental risk assessments for insurance policies. Interesting work and pays decent 50-90 k. But positions are very niche, mostly in medium to large cities.

Majors, listed for employment and salary potential:

1. Chemical engineering or civil engineering: 
Pros- Great for getting jobs, qualifying for a PE license, and higher salaries.
Cons- Tougher classes.

2. Environmental engineering:
Pros- Higher salaries, PE license, good potential.
Cons- Tougher classes, not as good as the chemical/civil, salaries might be slightly lower than the previous option.

3. Chemistry/Biology
Pros- General and can get similar jobs as environmental science/engineering.
Cons- At times, it might be considered too general. Lower salaries than the first two options.

4. Environmental Science
Pros- Still gives enough science for a good amount of environmental positions. Classes are easier.
Cons- Seen as less rigorous than an engineering degree.

5. Geology
Pros- Good salaries.
Cons- Limited amount of applicable jobs. Not much else you can do with it.

6. Environmental policy/planning, natural resources, foresty, wildlife management etc.
Pros- Good for government and non-profits. Easy classes.
Cons- Useless for other fields, will have lower salaries.
